claims.text: The reported nanoscale catalyst has exceptional activity in ethanol oxidation.
The baseline catalyst is predominantly composed of platinum-group metals and has a typical Pt-rich surface.
A synergistic electronic effect from alloying with secondary metals governs the catalyst's ethanol-oxidation performance.
Introducing or varying a secondary metal can alter the catalyst's surface electronic structure.
Introducing or varying a secondary metal will intentionally shift the catalyst's d-band center.
A shifted d-band center alters the adsorption and desorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Polymetallic alloying produces ligand effects that optimize the surface electronic structure.
Alloying alters ensemble effects and creates a distribution of active surface sites.
Ethanol oxidation on the catalyst follows an unusual Sabatier-type relationship with an optimal intermediate-binding regime.
Intermediate binding that is strong enough for conversion but weak enough for desorption sustains catalytic activity and selectivity.
Timely desorption of ethanol-oxidation intermediates minimizes site poisoning and promotes durability.
Changing the alloy composition will produce a measurable shift in ethanol-oxidation onset potential.
Changing the alloy composition will produce quantifiable changes in ethanol-oxidation current density or turnover frequency.
The compositionally modified catalyst will show improved tolerance to deactivation over time relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies when intermediate adsorption energies lie near an optimal Sabatier balance.
Very high temperatures or strong poisons can disrupt the proposed adsorption-energy balance and cause the mechanism to fail.
